scenes.text: Your body makes new cells all the time, to grow, to repair damage and to replace cells that wear out.
It does this in a series of stages called the cell cycle.
Inside this cell the nucleus holds the chromosomes, and in body cells they come in pairs.
First the cell grows and makes more of the structures inside it, such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
Then the DNA is copied, so each chromosome becomes two identical copies, joined together.
Now mitosis begins, and the membrane around the nucleus breaks down.
Fine fibres stretch out from each end of the cell and take hold of the chromosomes.
The chromosomes line up in a row across the middle of the cell.
The fibres pull the copies apart, so one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell.
A new membrane forms around each set, so the nucleus has divided.
Finally the cytoplasm and the cell membrane divide, making two cells.
Each new cell has the same chromosomes as the cell it came from, which is how the body grows and repairs itself.
